title: Fixed seven-day windows retain faster post-1997 stream recession at 114 south-east Australian catchments
abstract: We test whether variable measurement duration explains a reported stream recession rise. We use CAMELS-AUS v2.03 daily flow at the same 114 south-east Australian catchments as the prior whole-run study. We reproduce its gauge estimates within 0.00000022 log units. With flow and month controls and a 1951-1996 reference, the first seven retained days give rate increases of 36.9% in 1997-2009 (95% spatial limits 26.1-51.7%) and 25.0% in 2010-2021 (16.7-34.9%). The last seven days give 27.2% and 19.7%. Run-duration controls remove only 4.8% and 9.3% of the whole-run log changes. A stricter test uses identical events and dates for all horizons. It retains first-window increases of 34.8% and 23.3%, and last-window increases of 26.9% and 20.2%. In 1997-2009, the last-window era multiplier is 5.9% smaller than the first-window multiplier (3.4-8.7%). Thus changes in run duration do not explain the rise in this selected event set. The result supports a change across these declining-flow runs, but does not identify a change in aquifer properties. Monotonic flow does not imply no rain or recharge. Horizons can overlap. Limits resample 12 spatial cells and hold years and event selection fixed. This test does not address the century-scale record or establish the cause of annual runoff loss.

display.caption: Fixed windows retain a rate rise. Blue marks show the planned comparisons. Orange marks use identical events and midpoint dates across horizons. Bars show spatial 95% limits. All estimates use the same 114 gauges in 12 spatial cells.

citations.reason: Supplies the fixed gauge sample and the whole-run estimates that we reproduce and test.
Already tests dry-spell age. We test a distinct measurement horizon in maximal monotonic runs.
Shows that the result depends on the chosen recession measure; a rank test has a different target.
